title.en: Homage on both sides: bands, crafts and hunters

summary: Seventeen yajus, each with homage on both sides (namaḥ … ca vo namaḥ), completing the series begun in the third anuvāka. Pairs of beings are saluted and then addressed as ‘you’: women who wound and who crush, troops and their lords, the misshapen and the many-formed, great and small, those with and without chariots, then armies, charioteers and the crafts — carpenters, chariot-makers, potters, smiths — and the hunters, fowlers, fishermen, arrow- and bow-makers, dog-leaders and dogs. Sāyaṇa sums up the anuvāka as praise of Rudra chiefly in the forms of beings of many kinds, after the divine forms of the second and the thieves of the third.

ā + vyādhin ‘piercing’ (from √vyadh ‘to pierce’ with the agent suffix -in), feminine in -ī. A prefixed derivative, not a compound. Dative with namaḥ.

Enclitic: it never opens a clause. Here dative plural, governed by the closing namaḥ.

translation.literal: Homage to [the women] who wound from every side, and to [the women] who pierce in many ways — to you homage.
translation.readable: Homage to you who wound from every side and to you who pierce in many ways; to you, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa begins by placing the anuvāka: the third anuvāka gave yajus with homage on both sides, and the fourth gives others of the same kind («कानिचिदुभयतोनमस्काराणि यजूंषि»). He takes the āvyādhinīs as female forms able to pierce all round («आ समन्ताद्वेद्धुं शक्ताः») and the vividhyantīs as those able to pierce in a special way («विशेषेण वेद्धुं शक्ता»), and ends each gloss with the homage to them («ताभ्यो नमः»).
units.reflection: The yajus salutes the one who wounds before it names anything else. The address turns at the end to ‘you’: what is feared is spoken to, not only spoken of.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa’s gloss on the women’s forms is printed as स्रीमूर्तय, evidently for strīmūrtayaḥ ‘female forms’, and the participle as विवध्यन्त्यः for the mantra’s vividhyantyaḥ; the reading of the mantra is not in doubt.

vyakarana.note: A yajus with homage on both sides (ubhayato-namaskāra): namaḥ opens it and ca vo namaḥ closes it. The enclitic vaḥ (for yuṣmabhyam, P. 8.1.21) is a dative plural, ‘to you’, and takes up the two datives before it: ‘homage to A and to B — to you homage’.

Feminine dative plural of an ā-stem, agreeing with the feminine participle that follows. Sāyaṇa reads the first member as ut ‘up, high’ (उत्कृष्ट); Monier-Williams asks whether the word is corrupted from ud-gaṇa or uru-gaṇa and glosses ‘consisting of extended troops’.

√tṛh (tṛṃh) ‘to crush’, 7th class; the weak stem tṛṃh- with the participial -at, feminine -atī (Monier-Williams records the feminine tṛṃhatī). The text writes the Taittirīya ँ before h (तृँह); the padaccheda uses the ordinary anusvāra.

translation.literal: Homage to [the women] in troops, and to [the women] who crush — to you homage.
translation.readable: Homage to you who go in troops and to you who crush; to you, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes the ugaṇās as women of the highest troops, the Seven Mothers and the like («सप्तमातृकाद्याः»), and the tṛṃhatīs as fierce goddesses able to do harm («हिंसितुं समर्था»), Durgā and the others («दुर्गाद्या उग्रदेवताः»).

flags.note: W1 accents तृँह॒तीभ्य॑श्च (anudātta on ha, svarita on bhyaś); W2 prints the word with no marks (तृँहतीभ्यश्). The edition keeps W1’s accents; the unit is under svara review.
The form of ugaṇa is not secure: Sāyaṇa explains u- as ut ‘highest’ (उत्कृष्टगणरूपाः), Monier-Williams suggests a corruption of ud-gaṇa or uru-gaṇa. The samāsa entry follows Sāyaṇa.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa explains the gṛtsas as those given to craving, «विषयलम्पटा इत्यर्थः» — greedy for the objects of the senses — and the gṛtsapatis as those who protect them («तेषां पालका गृत्सपतयः»).

flags.note: The dictionaries give gṛtsa as ‘clever, sharp’; Sāyaṇa takes it as ‘greedy for sense-objects’ (his first word is printed गर्वनशीला, which may stand for gardhanaśīlāḥ ‘given to greed’). The word table gives both.

units.traditional: The printed bhāṣya has no comment on this yajus. Its numbering passes from the fourth yajus (vrāta) to a ‘fifth’ («पञ्चमं यजुराह») that is the yajus on the misshapen and the many-formed, which stands sixth here. Sāyaṇa’s reading of the anuvāka as a whole applies: Rudra praised in the forms of beings of many kinds («नानाजातिमूर्ति»).

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the virūpas are those of altered form («विरूपा विकृतरूपा»), the naked, the shaven-headed and the like («नग्नमुण्डादयः»); the viśvarūpas are attendants who bear forms of every kind, with the faces of horses, elephants and others («तुरंगगजवक्त्रादिनानाविधरूपधारिणो भृत्याः»). He numbers this yajus the fifth (पञ्चमं), one less than its place here; see the note on the previous yajus.

The Taittirīya text, and Sāyaṇa’s gloss, have -ṣṭa. Monier-Williams enters the word as puñji-ṣṭha (from the Vājasaneyi recension), ‘a fisherman or a bird-catcher’, a compound with -stha. Because the form here differs, no samāsa analysis is given.
ni-ṣāda, from ni + √sad; the name of a non-Āryan people described as hunters and fishermen (Monier-Williams). A prefixed derivative, not a compound.

translation.literal: Homage to the fowlers, and to the Niṣādas — to you homage.
translation.readable: Homage to you, the bird-catchers, and to you, the Niṣāda fishermen; to you, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa treats the ninth to the seventeenth yajus as clear («स्पष्टार्थानि») but glosses two words here: the puñjiṣṭas are killers of flocks of birds («पक्षिपुञ्जानां धातकाः», where धातकाः evidently stands for ghātakāḥ, ‘killers’), and the Niṣādas are killers of fish («मत्स्यघातिनो निषादाः»).

flags.note: puñjiṣṭa (text, Sāyaṇa) against puñjiṣṭha (Monier-Williams, from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā). The text is not altered; the analysis of the word as a compound is left open.
Sāyaṇa’s gloss is printed धातकाः; the sense ‘killers’ (ghātaka) is inferred from the context and from his gloss on niṣāda in the next sentence.

vyakarana.note: A yajus with homage on both sides (ubhayato-namaskāra): namaḥ opens it and ca vo namaḥ closes it. The enclitic vaḥ (for yuṣmabhyam, P. 8.1.21) is a dative plural, ‘to you’, and takes up the two datives before it: ‘homage to A and to B — to you homage’. Here the closing namaḥ ends the anuvāka and keeps its visarga before the pause (॥).

translation.literal: Homage to the dogs, and to the lords of dogs — to you homage.
translation.readable: Homage to you, the dogs, and to you, the masters of dogs; to you, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa treats this yajus as clear: he introduces the ninth to the seventeenth together as plain in meaning («नवममारभ्य सप्तदशपर्यन्तानि स्पष्टार्थानि यजूंष्याह») and adds nothing on this one. He closes the anuvāka by dividing the three: the second praises Rudra chiefly in the forms of deities taken for play («लीलार्थदेवतामूर्तिप्राधान्येन»), the third chiefly in the forms of thieves («चोरमूर्तिप्राधान्येन»), and the fourth chiefly in the forms of beings of many kinds («नानाजातिमूर्तिप्राधान्य»).
units.reflection: The anuvāka ends with dogs and those who keep them. Nothing in the list is too low to be named and bowed to.
